```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)

# Selected results transcribed from Zachreson et al. (2021), Table II.
# These are published simulation summaries, not newly simulated data.

growth_results <- data.frame(
  scenario = c(
    "Targeted interventions only",
    "10M priority vaccinations",
    "10M priority + 10.7M general vaccinations"
  ),
  growth_rate = c(0.118, 0.085, 0.057)
)

growth_results$scenario <- factor(
  growth_results$scenario,
  levels = rev(growth_results$scenario)
)

control_results <- data.frame(
  `Modelled condition` = c(
    "Targeted interventions alone",
    "Targeted interventions plus 10M priority and 10.7M general vaccinations"
  ),
  `Mean early growth rate per day` = c(
    "0.118",
    "0.057"
  ),
  `Approximate distancing-compliance threshold` = c(
    "Between 60% and 70%",
    "About 40%"
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

growth_reduction <- round(
  100 * (1 - 0.057 / 0.118)
)
```

Think back to the early vaccine rollout. One question loomed large: would vaccination mean the end of lockdowns?

A 2021 study in Australia using models suggested that a much better response than an “yes” or “no” was that vaccines would help to control outbreaks by slowing them down, even though they could not prevent transmission [@zachreson2021].

::: {.callout-note}
## A historical study, not today's forecast

This post explains scenarios developed in early 2021. It is not current vaccination or travel advice, and its numerical thresholds should not be transferred to today's variants, immunity levels or policies.
:::

## The problem: does protection have to be all or nothing?

It’s natural to think of vaccination in terms of a switch: you achieve a certain percentage, and then the restrictions don’t need to exist anymore. However, reducing transmission is useful even when not completely shutting the switch off.

The questions are how much slower an outbreak becomes, and how much additional distancing might still be needed to suppress it.

Agent-based modelling of Australia was carried out by Cameron Zachreson et al to answer those questions. The simulation did not treat all individuals as the same but considered different ages and their interactions at homes, school, etc.
[@zachreson2021].

## What did the researchers actually compare?

The data is based on simulations of an outbreak, not on a study where different restrictions were imposed on Australians in a controlled experiment. The simulation incorporated demographic data from Australia, including the 2016 Census.

Vaccination was distributed before any outbreaks occurred, and older people were given priority. The model did not simulate the vaccine distribution occurring during an outbreak.

The study authors combined the higher efficacy priority vaccine with the lower efficacy general vaccine, along with travel restrictions and isolation of those infected.They also variedpopulation-wide distancing.

For estimating growth early on, they conducted 110 simulations for each scenario [@zachreson2021].

The following figure and table show selected summary statistics from the paper. They do not rerun the original model.

## Slower growth still matters

@fig-growth displays the mean growth rate of outbreaks for three selected cases. Vaccination helped to reduce the growth rate of outbreaks; however, it could not make it negative.

```{r}
#| label: fig-growth
#| fig-cap: "Figure 1: Growth rates during the early epidemic for selected scenarios. Three scenarios are all with targeted interventions. Re-drawn from Table II of Zachreson et al. (2021); these are simulations, not reported case numbers. Bars represent selected mean values; uncertainty is addressed below."
#| fig-alt: "There are three horizontal bars indicating the growth rates of 0.118 per day when only targeted interventions are used, 0.085 with 10 million priority vaccinations, and 0.057 with 10 million priority and 10.7 million general vaccinations."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| out-width: "100%"

growth_plot <- ggplot(
  growth_results,
  aes(x = growth_rate, y = scenario)
) +
  geom_col(
    width = 0.58,
    fill = "#087e8b"
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = sprintf("%.3f", growth_rate)),
    hjust = -0.2,
    size = 4.3,
    colour = "#253343"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 0.135),
    breaks = seq(0, 0.12, by = 0.03),
    labels = function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete(
    labels = c(
      "10M priority + 10.7M general vaccinations" =
        "10M priority +\n10.7M general",
      "10M priority vaccinations" =
        "10M priority",
      "Targeted interventions only" =
        "Targeted interventions\nonly"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Slower growth, not zero growth",
    subtitle = "Selected 2021 model scenarios",
    x = "Mean early epidemic growth rate per day",
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Source: Zachreson et al. (2021), Table II."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      colour = "#173e59",
      size = 18
    ),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(
      colour = "#43556a",
      margin = margin(b = 12)
    ),
    axis.text = element_text(colour = "#253343"),
    axis.title.x = element_text(
      colour = "#253343",
      margin = margin(t = 10)
    ),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = "#d7e0e8"),
    plot.caption = element_text(
      colour = "#43556a",
      hjust = 0,
      margin = margin(t = 12)
    ),
    plot.background = element_rect(
      fill = "#f8fafc",
      colour = NA
    ),
    panel.background = element_rect(
      fill = "#f8fafc",
      colour = NA
    ),
    plot.margin = margin(12, 18, 12, 12)
  )

growth_plot
```

With maximum coverage, the mean value reduced from 0.118 to 0.057 per day, which is about `r growth_reduction` lower.

This represents a decline in the rate of growth rather than an assertion that there were `r growth_reduction`% fewer infections, or that each individual’s probability was `r growth_reduction`% lower.

This model thus suggests a compromise approach – the disease may continue to spread but at a much slower pace. This explains why the failure to achieve total herd immunity does not necessarily mean failure of the vaccination program.

## What changed for lockdowns?

The researchers then applied population-wide distancing once the cumulative incidence was 2,000 cases. They estimated how much compliance was needed for outbreaks to move towards suppression.

@tbl-controls brings the selected growth and distancing findings together.

::: {.table-scroll}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-controls
#| tbl-cap: "Table 1: Vaccination reduced early growth and compliance required for suppression. Data from Zachreson et al. (2021), Table II and Section III C"
#| tbl-colwidths: [46, 22, 32]

knitr::kable(
  control_results,
  align = c("l", "r", "l"),
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

:::

Compliance refers to the model's distancing behaviour, not a percentage reduction in legal restrictions.

The highest-coverage scenario represented approximately 88% population coverage. It is not a universal target. The thresholds depend on the vaccines, allocation, contact patterns and other controls used in the simulation.

Nor does “about 40%” mean governments could simply remove 60% of their rules. It is a model-specific estimate of population compliance with specified distancing measures.

## Why the qualifications matter

There was no herd immunity threshold evident in the various feasible scenarios of hybrid rollout that the researchers looked at. Contact networks and age-based distribution were significant, especially clustering of kids in schools.

Impact of the vaccines on transmission was also not established [@zachreson2021].

The chart shows selected means, not the full uncertainty. For example, the paper reports 5th–95th percentile ranges of 0.110–0.127 per day for targeted interventions alone and 0.052–0.062 for the highest-coverage scenario.

Those ranges describe variation between simulated outbreaks. They are not the same as confidence intervals for the estimated mean.

The study answers a transmission question under assumptions. It does not settle which restrictions would be socially acceptable, economically worthwhile, or appropriate today.

## The takeaway: fewer restrictions is different from no restrictions

The opening question was whether vaccination would remove the need for lockdowns.

In these 2021 scenarios, not reliably, but it reduced early growth and the amount of distancing needed to suppress an outbreak.

It is not a specific percentage, but the idea that different protections can interact to reinforce each other. One protection might lighten the load for another, without either making risk go away completely [@zachreson2021].
